messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh is a 60-year-old fisherman who has spent most of his life in the coastal waters of Oregon, working alongside his son Hao. Five years ago, during a late autumn storm, a rogue wave swept Hao overboard while they were hauling nets. Minh dove into the churning water, but the current was too strong; he could not find his son. The crew was slow to launch a rescue dinghy, and by the time they did, Hao had disappeared. Minh was pulled back aboard, shivering and voiceless. He survived. His son did not.

In the weeks that followed, Minh tried to return to the boat, but every time the hull groaned against a swell, his chest tightened, his breath came short, and a cold sweat broke across his forehead. He began to feel a deadness inside, a hollow where grief should have been. He would sit at the dinner table with his wife, staring at his plate, unable to feel anything except a dull, grinding guilt that pressed on his chest like a physical weight. He told himself that Hao had trusted him, and he had failed. The other fishermen on the crew, Minh decided, were not to be trusted—they had hesitated, they had been slow, they had let his son die. He began to see their glances as accusations, their silences as judgment.

The guilt did not stay quiet. Each time Minh’s heart raced at the sound of waves against the pier, he interpreted it as evidence that he was weak, that he did not deserve to be alive when Hao was dead. The physical panic became a confirmation of his unworthiness, and that belief only made the panic worse. When he lay awake at night, the memory of the storm would replay, and his own body would respond as if he were still in the water—trembling, gasping, drenched in sweat. These episodes would then flood him with rage at himself and at the crew, and with a fresh wave of shame. Why had he not done more? Why had he been the one pulled back onto the boat? His wife would reach for him, but he felt only mistrust—could she really understand, or would she also judge him? So he withdrew, the numbness growing deeper.

Over the years, Minh stopped stepping onto the docks altogether. He told his wife he was too old, but the truth was that the sight of the boats triggered the same physical reaction every time: his stomach would drop, his palms would sweat, and he would feel the old guilt surge. He took up small repair work on land, but the sound of foghorns or the smell of salt air could still send him into a state of jittery vigilance. His sleep remained broken; he often woke at 3 a.m. with his heart pounding, convinced he had heard Hao calling. These episodes would then reinforce his sense that he was being punished, that he had failed in the most fundamental duty of a father. The more his body reacted, the more he believed he was guilty, and the more guilty he felt, the more his body reacted. It became a closed loop that he could not escape.

He avoided talking about Hao, avoided the photos his wife kept on the mantle, avoided the annual ceremony at the harbor. He came to see his own emotional deadness as a kind of protection—if he felt nothing, he could not be destroyed again. Yet the guilt and the physical fear remained, gnawing at him in quiet moments. His wife finally insisted he see a clinician after she found him sobbing on the bathroom floor, unable to explain why. Minh agreed reluctantly, not because he believed therapy would help, but because he was exhausted. He is most afraid that speaking about it will prove once and for all that he is to blame, that he will hear the words aloud and find no mercy in them. But beneath that fear, a small part of him hopes for something he cannot name—perhaps a way to feel something other than guilt, a way to trust the ground beneath his feet again.
